title: Hand of Straights
description: Brute force to optimized: an explicit backtracking framing versus recognizing the greedy choice is provably forced, enabling direct greedy consumption.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Alice has a hand of cards, each with an integer value. She wants to rearrange the cards into groups so that each group has exactly groupSize cards, and each group consists of groupSize CONSECUTIVE integer values. Return true if this is possible.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Partition into groups of consecutive values\"","Count occurrences, then greedily consume consecutive runs starting from the smallest remaining value"],["A count-based feasibility check","A hash map of value counts, combined with sorted unique values, drives the greedy consumption"]]}

blocks.text: Since every group must be groupSize consecutive values, the SMALLEST value remaining in the hand can only ever be the START of a group (it can never be the middle or end of a group, since that would require an even smaller value to exist, which would then itself need to start its own group first). This forces a deterministic greedy strategy.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting a Deck into Consecutive Straights, Starting from the Lowest Card
blocks.text: Picture sorting playing cards (of various duplicate values) into groups that each form a straight run of a fixed length. The lowest remaining card in the deck must always begin a new straight, since nothing smaller exists to have started one for it; following this rule strictly and checking feasibility at each step determines whether a full valid grouping exists.

blocks.caption: The smallest remaining value must always start a new group, since nothing smaller could have consumed it as a later member

blocks.text: Result: true. Groups [1,2,3], [2,3,4], [6,7,8] use every card exactly once, each a valid consecutive run of size 3.

Before trying every possible way to partition the hand, notice that the smallest remaining value is FORCED to start a new group (nothing smaller exists to place it elsewhere), which makes the entire process deterministic: repeatedly take the smallest remaining value, consume it and the next groupSize-1 consecutive values, and fail immediately if any of them are unavailable.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If groupSize does not evenly divide the hand's total size, it is immediately impossible to form complete groups, so this check can be done first as a quick rejection.

Observation 2: Counting occurrences of each value, and looking at the SMALLEST value with a remaining positive count, that value must start a group, since no smaller value exists to have already "used it up" as a later member of an earlier group.

Observation 3: Once a starting value is identified, that many copies of it (specifically, however many are needed to fully consume its available count in properly-sized batches, though in practice this greedy takes the count first appearing) forces the SAME number of consecutive values (start, start+1, ..., start+groupSize-1) to also be consumed at least that many times; if any of these values lacks sufficient count, the hand cannot be validly grouped.

Observation 4: Repeating this process (always starting from the current smallest remaining positive-count value) until all counts reach zero, or a required value runs out, determines feasibility.

This leads to counting occurrences per value, then repeatedly starting a group at the smallest remaining positive-count value, consuming that count from each of the next groupSize consecutive values, failing immediately if any is insufficient.
Try every possible way to partition the hand into groups of groupSize, checking whether each group forms a valid consecutive run.

items: Recursively pick groupSize cards from the remaining hand to form the next group.
Check if the picked cards, when sorted, form a consecutive run.
If a full valid partition is found, return true; if all attempts fail, return false.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Explicitly trying to form each group and backtracking on failure directly implements the problem's literal grouping requirement.

Since the smallest remaining value is always FORCED to start the next group (no other valid choice exists), this framing does no real additional search, but naming it explicitly as a brute-force / backtracking approach clarifies why the greedy version below is not actually a "heuristic," it is the ONLY valid choice at each step.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for the sorted map operations, similar to the optimized version since the choice is forced (no true branching).
Space: O(n) for the count map.

Limitation: since the smallest remaining value is always forced to start the next group, there is no actual backtracking needed; recognizing this determinism directly, without any exploratory framing, leads to the clean greedy solution.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why there is no real "search" here: the smallest remaining value with a positive count has no other valid role except starting a new group, since nothing smaller exists to consume it as a later group member.

The greedy consumption rule: maintain a count map; repeatedly find the smallest value with a positive count, then consume that same count from each of the next groupSize consecutive values (start, start+1, ..., start+groupSize-1), failing immediately if any lacks sufficient count.

Efficient implementation: sorting the distinct values once, then processing them in order (skipping any already fully consumed), avoids repeatedly searching for "the current smallest" from scratch.

The core idea: since the greedy choice is forced (not just convenient), directly implementing it, without any exploratory backtracking, is both correct and efficient.

Count occurrences per value. Sort distinct values. For each in order (if its count is still positive), consume that count from it and the next groupSize-1 consecutive values, failing if any lacks sufficient count.

blocks.caption: Greedily consume consecutive runs starting from the smallest remaining value each time

blocks.text: Since the smallest remaining value can only ever be the start of a group (no smaller value exists to have consumed it earlier), the greedy process of always starting a new group there, and consuming exactly its count from the next groupSize-1 consecutive values as well, correctly and deterministically follows the ONLY valid grouping strategy. If at any point a required consecutive value has insufficient count, no valid grouping can exist, since that group starting position was forced and had no alternative.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), for building and iterating the sorted count map.
Space: O(n) for the count map.

blocks.text: Hand of Straights demonstrates a greedy choice that is not just convenient but PROVABLY FORCED: the smallest remaining value has no valid alternative role, making the entire algorithm deterministic once this is recognized.

Not skipping already-fully-consumed values when iterating the sorted keys, potentially redoing work (though this does not affect correctness if guarded by a "need > 0" check).

blocks.text: Explicitly proving WHY the smallest remaining value must start a group (no smaller value exists to place it otherwise) is the key insight that justifies the greedy approach as provably correct, not just a heuristic.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "partition into groups of consecutive values", think: the smallest remaining value is forced to start each new group; consume greedily and check feasibility.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the explicit backtracking framing and the direct greedy approach run in O(n log n) time and O(n) space, since the greedy choice is provably forced with no real branching to explore.

items: Pattern: a provably forced greedy choice, since the smallest remaining value has no valid alternative role except starting a new group.
Core Idea: repeatedly consume the smallest remaining value's count from it and the next groupSize-1 consecutive values, failing if any lacks sufficient count.
Time: O(n log n) for both the explicit and direct greedy framings.
Most Important Observation: the smallest remaining value can only ever start a group, making the entire process deterministic.
Interview Difficulty: a clean greedy problem rewarding a rigorous proof of why the greedy choice is forced, not just convenient.
One line memory trick: the smallest remaining value always starts a group; consume its count from the next groupSize consecutive values.
